units.title: State-machine replication and safety versus liveness
outcomes: Explain how an agreed command prefix and deterministic execution produce replicated state.
Separate election safety, log matching and state-machine safety from conditional progress.
State the crash-recovery, storage and timing assumptions behind your consensus contract.
units.why: Build on Replication, quorums and consensus vocabulary. Here the contract becomes a ledger of properties that every later Raft transition must preserve, not another survey of replication styles.

next.note: Turn the contract into election transitions.

study.title: Raft extended paper (20 May 2014): replication contract
study.locator: Section 2, Replicated state machines, and Figure 1; Figure 3, Raft guarantees; Section 5.6, Timing and availability
study.depth: Read the guarantees as obligations to justify later. Skip the Paxos comparison and the evaluation for now.

study.title: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3: module boundary
study.locator: Introduction, Getting Started and The code, through the description of `labrpc`
study.depth: Inspect the interface and public tests. Begin implementation in the election unit; keep course solutions private.

focus: Replicas at different applied indexes need not have identical current state. Equal initial state and an equal deterministic command prefix imply equal state at that prefix.
Uncommitted suffixes may differ. State-machine safety forbids different commands being applied at the same index, not temporary differences between whole logs.

Basic Raft safety assumes correct protocol execution and stable storage across crashes, not bounded message delay. Progress also needs a communicating majority and sufficiently stable timing and leadership.
A safety counterexample has a finite bad prefix. A bounded interval without commits is evidence of a stall, not a proof of permanent nontermination.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, draw the client, consensus module, log and state machine from Figure 1. Trace an append through local acceptance, durable replication, commitment, application and reply. Mark which boundaries the Lab 3 interface exposes and which belong to the service. Classify a conflicting applied command as a safety violation and a minority partition with no completed writes as a progress stall.
traps: Treating `Start()` returning as a successful client write. It starts agreement; it does not promise commitment.
Putting local randomness or wall-clock reads inside the deterministic application transition instead of agreeing their results as command data.
Reading the paper's availability summary as an unconditional termination theorem for any network with a connected majority. Timing and competing elections still matter.

selfTest.q: Two replicas have applied different-length prefixes. Must their current states match?
selfTest.a: No. Compare state after the same prefix. A lagging replica can be safe while behind.

selfTest.q: Can a safe log contain different commands at one index on different servers?
selfTest.a: Yes, in uncommitted suffixes. They must not both become applied decisions at that index.

selfTest.q: Does a timeout establish that the leader crashed?
selfTest.a: No. It creates suspicion. Safety must survive false suspicion; progress needs additional timing and communication assumptions.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `loglab` invariant ledger, fault-model statement and separate acceptance, persistence, commit, apply and reply events.
units.stopWhen: Your ledger names a finite witness for each safety property and states the assumptions needed for progress without requiring identical uncommitted logs.

fit.note: The paper supplies the precise contract and timing boundary; the lab interface and mini-project make the abstraction boundaries observable.

units.title: Terms and epochs, follower, candidate and leader states and randomized election timeouts
outcomes: Implement follower, candidate and leader transitions with monotonic terms.
Justify at most one elected leader per term using persistent votes and majority intersection.
Diagnose repeated elections without weakening voting rules.
units.why: The election state machine establishes authority for one term. Randomized timeouts help establish that authority promptly; they do not make conflicting votes safe.

next.note: Add log freshness and examine election recovery.

study.locator: Sections 5.1 and 5.2; Figure 2 election state and rules; Figures 4 and 5

study.title: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3A: leader election
study.locator: Part 3A: leader election, including heartbeat limits and election timeout guidance

focus: On an election timeout, increment the term, vote for yourself, reset the randomized election timer and send vote requests. Count distinct voters only for the election still in progress.
In basic Raft, a higher term in either an RPC request or response makes a candidate or leader update its term and become a follower. A stale response must not resurrect an old election.
A candidate receiving same-term AppendEntries becomes a follower. A term need not elect any leader, and servers need not observe term changes simultaneously.
Reset election timers for the Figure 2 events, not every incoming packet. Choose timeout and heartbeat spacing for the lab's limits rather than copying the paper's example milliseconds.
units.reproduce: From a blank page, trace three followers in term 0. Let one time out, enter term 1, vote for itself and receive a second distinct vote: it becomes leader. Deliver that second vote again: the count must not increase. Then deliver a response carrying term 2: the leader becomes a term-2 follower. Implement this transition trace alongside Lab 3A on your machine.
traps: Claiming there can never be two servers that think they are leader. The invariant is one elected leader per term, not instant agreement across terms.
Resetting the timer on a rejected stale vote request, allowing an obsolete sender to suppress progress.
Reading replies after unlocking and applying them without checking that the role and term still match the RPC's election.

selfTest.q: Why can two different candidates not each win term 7 in a fixed configuration?
selfTest.a: Their majorities intersect, and the intersecting server cannot vote for both in term 7, including across a restart.

selfTest.q: Does a candidate step down on same-term AppendEntries?
selfTest.a: Yes. It recognizes the elected leader for that term. A stale-term AppendEntries is rejected instead.

selfTest.q: Do identical election timeouts threaten safety or progress?
selfTest.a: Progress: simultaneous candidates may repeatedly split the vote. Correct majority and one-vote rules still preserve election safety.

practice.name: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3A: leader election
practice.locator: Part 3A; `TestInitialElection3A`, `TestReElection3A` and `TestManyElections3A`; run `make RUN="-run 3A" raft1` from `src`
practice.note: Use the public tests locally with Go and the race detector through the supplied Make target. They exercise initial election and elections under disconnection and reconnection, not disk durability. Keep solutions private.

units.stopWhen: Lab 3A passes, and your explicit trace ignores a duplicate vote and steps down on a higher-term reply without accepting delayed votes from the old election.

fit.note: The paper derives election safety and the lab provides bounded local implementation practice with public network-failure tests.

units.title: The RequestVote freshness rule, split votes, pre-vote and leadership transfer
outcomes: Implement the term-first, index-second vote freshness comparison.
Walk a split vote through a later successful election without double voting.
Explain what pre-vote and leadership transfer change, and which safety checks they retain.
units.why: Election safety alone can elect a server missing committed history. Freshness connects election to log safety; the optional mechanisms address avoidable disruptions rather than replacing that rule.

next.note: Preserve matching prefixes when the elected leader replicates.
Use freshness in the leader-completeness argument.

study.title: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lab 3B: election prerequisite
study.locator: Part 3B: log, instruction to implement the Section 5.4.1 election restriction
study.depth: Add freshness to the existing election code. Finish replication in the following units.

focus: Compare `lastLogTerm` first, then `lastLogIndex` only when terms tie. Neither total log length nor the candidate's election term substitutes for its last entry's term.
Freshness is necessary but not sufficient for granting a vote: the request term and the recorded vote still constrain the decision.
Pre-vote asks whether a prospective election could win before incrementing the local term. An isolated node cannot repeatedly advance its term just by timing out under this extension.
Leadership transfer catches up the target, stops accepting new work during transfer and triggers a normal new-term election with `TimeoutNow`. It does not appoint a leader without votes.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compare logs by their last entry. A voter ends at index 10 in log term 3. A candidate ending at index 6 in log term 4 passes freshness; one ending at index 20 in log term 2 fails; one ending at index 9 in log term 3 fails. Assume the RPC election term is acceptable and no other vote was cast. Then draw a three-candidate split vote and a later term in which one candidate obtains two distinct votes.
traps: Granting a vote to a longer log whose last entry has an older term.
Treating a pre-vote response as a durable vote or changing the current term merely because a prospective term is mentioned.
Assuming pre-vote cures all membership disruptions or guarantees progress under arbitrary partitions. It addresses a particular rejoining-node disruption.

selfTest.q: A candidate has the same last log term and index as the voter. Is freshness satisfied?
selfTest.a: Yes. Equality passes freshness, but the voter must still satisfy the term and one-vote rules.

selfTest.q: Why may a shorter log be more up-to-date?
selfTest.a: Its last entry can have a newer term. Raft orders by last term before length; commitment safety also relies on the current-term commit restriction.

selfTest.q: Can leadership transfer succeed if the target cannot obtain a majority?
selfTest.a: No. The target must win an ordinary election. The proposed transfer aborts if it does not complete, rather than bypassing quorum rules.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: freshness cases, split-vote replay and stale-election replies in `loglab`; optional pre-vote and transfer schedules retain the same election and log invariants.
units.stopWhen: Your vote handler passes the three freshness cases, your split-vote trace recovers in a later term, and you can explain the optional extensions without treating them as new authority rules.

fit.note: The paper and lab supply freshness; the existing thesis companion fills the pre-vote and transfer gap, with implementation practice in the mini-project.
